title.narrative: Social productive integration in Colombia to improve food safety by the use of animal manure as a source of soil enrichment

description.narrative: Colombia has large amounts of soils used for agriculture and livestock farming, yet limited knowledge on circular farming is available, leading to unnecessary and excessive use of chemicals fertilizers which in turn has negative effects on the environment and communities. In particular those communities living in post-conflict areas where they heavily rely on farming to make a living. By transforming animal manure and organic waste into compost, these negative effects can decrease rapidly and value can be added for the farmers’ produce. Knowledge transfer and capacity building is necessary for this. The consortium of Hocotec, Wilschip and Nutrisuin is specialized in pig farming and have also established an agricultural education center. They have developed a technology that processes animal manure into usable organic compost which can offer a sustainable solution to current issues. To make it possible to further upscale the consortium’s current DGGF investment in Pig Farming and to create immediate impact for local farming communities, increasing production capacity and knowledge transfer are required. Therefore, Technical Assistance (DGGF) offers support for the development of a Agro-Social Production Training Project by the consortium in cooperation with La Universidad de la Salle. By providing training to local leaders of farming families and leading students of 50 rural towns on sustainable animal’s manure management and using organic compost for agriculture, the project will increase soil productivity, improve animal managing techniques and production yields and will lead to more sustainable production processes of approximately 2000 farmers in the area, which will have a positive impact on the environment and the communities these farmers are part of. Furthermore the project will study animal manure’s characteristics and quality and obtain relevant data about the most effective use of organic fertiliser for a variety of crops produced in those areas of which the results will be shared with farmers in the region and used to develop an agricultural course with together with the University. The project currently supports 8 direct jobs, 500 indirect jobs and has already provided training to 450 farmers and leading student. More impact is expected to be achieved during the next few months.
